title: White Nights
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
setting: St Petersburg in the season of the white nights: a canal embankment and a bench, the dreamer’s green-walled room and the grandmother’s little wooden house
lengthNote: Four nights and a morning, about 17,000 words; the second night gives way to Nastenka’s own story
openingLine: It was a wonderful night, such a night as is only possible when we are young, dear reader.
summary: A lonely young man who has lived in Petersburg for eight years without making a friend walks home one night along a canal and finds a girl crying at the railing. Over four nights he tells Nastenka what a dreamer is, she tells him about the lodger who promised to come back for her in a year, and he delivers her letter and falls in love with her. On the fourth night she agrees to marry him, and a minute later the lodger walks past. Dostoevsky called it a sentimental novel. It is a love story, and a close portrait of a man who has lived almost entirely on daydreams.
referenceStyle: the story’s own divisions: First Night, Second Night, Nastenka’s History, Third Night, Fourth Night and Morning

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of White Nights and Other Stories, translated by Constance Garnett (eBook 36034)
sourceText.note: Garnett’s translation of 1918, the tenth volume of her Novels of Fyodor Dostoevsky, which also contains Notes from Underground. It follows Dostoevsky’s revised text of 1860 and does not print his epigraph from Turgenev. Garnett spells the charwoman’s name two ways, Fekla and Fyokla; her spellings are kept.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In the journal Otechestvennye zapiski, dedicated to Dostoevsky’s friend the poet Aleksei Pleshcheyev, four months before both men were arrested.

atAGlance.label: Subtitle
atAGlance.note: From the reminiscences of a dreamer. Garnett calls it a sentimental story from the diary of a dreamer.

atAGlance.label: Revised
atAGlance.note: For Dostoevsky’s first collected works, when he added the long list of the dreamer’s romantic fantasies on the second night.

atAGlance.label: The narrator
atAGlance.note: A minor official who has lived eight years in Petersburg and knows its houses better than its people.

structure.label: First Night
structure.title: A girl at the canal railing
structure.summary: Petersburg has emptied for the summer and the narrator, who knows every face and house in it but no one to speak to, walks out beyond the city gates. Coming home late along the canal he sees a girl crying at the railing, rescues her with his knotted stick from a drunken gentleman, and walks her home. She agrees to meet him again the next night on one condition: he must not fall in love with her.

scenes.title: An empty city
scenes.summary: The old man on the Fontanka, the houses that talk to him, and the whole town leaving for its summer villas.

scenes.title: The canal embankment
scenes.summary: Tears at the railing, a staggering gentleman, the stick, and an appointment for ten o’clock the next night.

structure.label: Second Night
structure.title: What a dreamer is
structure.summary: Nastenka asks for his history, and he says he has none. Instead, speaking of himself in the third person, he describes a dreamer: a creature who hides in a corner, lives on romances, finds real visitors unbearable and wakes from his reveries to find that his best years have gone. Nastenka, who has been listening wide-eyed, is moved, and offers her own story in return for his advice.

scenes.title: I am a type
scenes.summary: The nooks of Petersburg, the dreamer like a snail in his shell, and a friend who calls once and never again.

scenes.title: The fantasies
scenes.summary: Hoffmann, Walter Scott’s heroines, Kazan and Danton; then the anniversaries he keeps for feelings that never happened.

structure.label: Nastenka’s History
structure.title: The lodger upstairs
structure.summary: Nastenka is seventeen and lives with her blind grandmother, who has pinned their dresses together for two years to keep her out of mischief. A young lodger lent them Walter Scott and Pushkin and took them to The Barber of Seville. When he was leaving for Moscow she went up to his room with her clothes in a bundle, and he promised to come back for her in a year if he could. He has been back in Petersburg three days and has not come. The narrator proposes a letter, and she hands him one she has already written.

scenes.title: The pinned dress
scenes.summary: The grandmother, the deaf charwoman who once took Nastenka’s place, and a new lodger who is pleasant looking.

scenes.title: The bundle
scenes.summary: Novels, the opera, a year’s promise, and a letter ready and sealed like Rosina’s.

structure.label: Third Night
structure.title: Waiting for the lodger
structure.summary: Written the next day, in rain. The narrator has delivered the letter, and on the third night Nastenka is happy, affectionate and full of plans; she likes him, she says, because he has not fallen in love with her. The lodger does not come. She wonders aloud why he cannot be more like the narrator, and why people cannot all be like brothers to one another, and she goes home promising to come back.

scenes.title: Rain
scenes.summary: A gloomy day, like the old age ahead of him, and the recollection of an evening spent waiting.

scenes.title: Eleven o’clock
scenes.summary: A bell counted aloud, false comfort, and a comparison of the two men.

structure.label: Fourth Night
structure.title: A proposal on the embankment
structure.summary: There is no letter, and Nastenka breaks down. The narrator tells her that he loves her; she says she will get over the lodger and accepts him, and they walk up and down planning to live together with her grandmother. Then a young man passes, stops and calls her name. She runs to him, runs back to kiss the narrator, and goes off with the lodger.

scenes.title: The confession
scenes.summary: Tears at the railing again, and the words it is impossible, but I love you.

scenes.title: The lodger returns
scenes.summary: Plans for the room upstairs and another trip to the opera, cut short by a voice behind them.

structure.label: Morning
structure.title: A letter and a clean ceiling
structure.summary: It is raining. Matrona brings a letter from Nastenka, who asks his forgiveness, calls him a brother and tells him she will be married next week. Matrona has swept away the cobwebs, and the room suddenly looks old; he sees himself fifteen years on, in the same room with the same servant. He blesses Nastenka, and asks whether a whole moment of happiness is too little for a lifetime.

characters.name: The dreamer
characters.role: The narrator, twenty-six and a minor official
characters.summary: He has lived in Petersburg for eight years and speaks to almost nobody, yet he nods to strangers he sees every day, greets the houses as friends and grieves when the town leaves for the summer. His real life happens in fantasies built out of Scott, Hoffmann and Pushkin, and he knows it; on the second night he describes his condition with painful accuracy, in the third person because he is ashamed. With Nastenka he is generous, funny and easily hurt. He delivers her letter to the man she loves, and when she chooses the lodger he blesses her.
characters.clue: He greets the houses of the city as friends, and could not bear to visit a pretty pink one after it had been painted yellow.

relationships.label: delivers a letter for, then loses to

characters.name: Nastenka
characters.role: Seventeen, living with her blind grandmother
characters.summary: Quick, frank and much braver than the narrator. She has spent two years pinned to her grandmother’s dress, read her way out through Walter Scott and Pushkin, and once went up to the lodger’s room with her clothes in a bundle. She sets the terms of the friendship on the first night, teases the narrator’s grand manner, and knows more about his feelings than she lets on. When the lodger does not come she turns to the narrator honestly, and when the lodger does come she goes straight to him. Her letter the next morning is loving, sincere and entirely on her own side.
characters.clue: For two years her dress was pinned to her grandmother’s, and a deaf charwoman once sat in her place so that she could slip out.

characters.name: The lodger
characters.role: The young man upstairs, gone to Moscow for a year
characters.summary: We see him only through Nastenka’s story and for a moment at the end. He is grave, poor and careful: he lends the family good novels, takes the grandmother and Nastenka to the opera, keeps his distance afterwards, and refuses to bind her with a promise he cannot keep. Whether he delays for three days out of doubt, business or indifference the story never says. He comes back, as he promised, and is to marry her within the week.
characters.clue: He took a blind old lady and her granddaughter to The Barber of Seville, and a year later passes a bench on the embankment at the worst possible moment.

characters.name: The grandmother
characters.summary: She owns the little wooden house, lives on her pension and the lodger’s rent, and remembers better days, when the sun was warmer and she sang Rosina in private theatricals. She pins Nastenka to her side and searches lent books for love letters, yet takes her to the opera and would like, it turns out, a young man upstairs. She is comic and a jailer, and Nastenka is fond of her.
characters.clue: Blind, she knits stockings, remembers when cream did not turn so sour, and tells her granddaughter to look under the bindings of novels for hidden love letters.

characters.name: Matrona
characters.summary: Matrona keeps his room, encourages the spider’s web on the ceiling and ignores his lectures about it. The dreamer says she has no imagination at all. On the last morning she brings Nastenka’s letter and announces that she has swept the cobwebs away, so he can have a wedding or a party; looking at her, he sees the fifteen solitary years ahead of him.
characters.clue: She cleans the ceiling of spider’s webs on the very morning her master learns that the girl he loves is marrying another man.

characters.name: Fyokla
characters.summary: Good-natured and very deaf, she once sat pinned to the grandmother in Nastenka’s place so that the girl could slip out to see a friend, and gave the game away when the old woman woke and asked her something she could not hear. Later it is through her that the lodger offers his books. Garnett calls her Fekla in that episode and Fyokla afterwards.
characters.clue: Unable to hear a question put to her by the old woman she was fastened to, she undid the pin and ran away.

themes.name: Dreaming and real life
themes.summary: Most of the narrator’s life happens in his imagination, and he says so. On the second night he describes a dreamer who hides in his corner, builds whole romances out of books and wakes to find the room dark and his years gone, and he calls this life a crime and a sin. Nastenka gives him four nights of real life, and the story shows that real life hurts in ways daydreams do not. His last words ask whether one moment of happiness is enough for a lifetime, and the story leaves the question open.
themes.development: A walk beyond the city gates; I make up regular romances in my dreams; the monologue of the second night; the anniversaries of feelings that never happened; the proposal; the cleaned ceiling.

themes.name: Loneliness
themes.summary: Eight years in a great city and hardly an acquaintance: the narrator knows faces and houses, but no one knows him. Nastenka is lonely in another way, pinned to a blind old woman with nobody to advise her. Their four nights are a meeting of two lonely people, and she puts the problem into words when she asks why people cannot all be like brothers. At the end he pictures himself in the same room fifteen years later, as solitary as before.
themes.development: The town leaving for its villas; the friend who visits once; the pinned dress; the bench by the canal; Matrona and the room grown old.

themes.name: St Petersburg
themes.summary: The city is the narrator’s only real acquaintance. Its houses talk to him, its summer departures make him feel abandoned, and its canals and embankments are where the whole story happens. The white nights of the title are the weeks around midsummer when the northern sky does not go fully dark, and they give the meetings their unreal light. When the weather turns, so does the story: the third night is written on a rainy day and the morning is wet and grey.
themes.development: The Nevsky, the Gardens and the Fontanka; villas on Kamenny Island and at Pargolovo; the canal railing; Nastenka’s side street; rain.

themes.name: Love and friendship
themes.summary: Nastenka offers friendship on condition that there is no love, and the narrator agrees at once; the rest of the story shows why the bargain cannot hold. The language of brothers and sisters runs all the way through: brotherly sympathy on the first night, brotherly advice on the second, more than brother and sister on the third, a friend and a brother in her final letter. It lets both of them name what they feel without naming it, until the fourth night, when he says it outright.
themes.development: You mustn’t fall in love with me; the letter carried to a rival; I like you because you have not fallen in love with me; the confession; If only you were he.

themes.name: The pinned dress
themes.summary: Nastenka’s grandmother pins the girl’s dress to her own so that she cannot go anywhere, and for two years the two sit together knitting, sewing and reading aloud. It is comic and it is a prison, and it explains why a girl of seventeen would climb the stairs to a lodger with her clothes in a bundle. The narrator is confined too, by habit and shyness to his corner, and the two confinements explain why they understand each other so quickly.
themes.development: The pin; the deaf charwoman sitting in her place; Walter Scott through the binding; the bundle on the lodger’s bed; the plan for the empty room upstairs.

themes.name: Reading and romance
themes.summary: Everyone in the story has learned about love from books. The narrator nearly says Madam! and stops because the word has been said a thousand times in society novels; his fantasies come from Scott, Hoffmann and Pushkin; Nastenka reads her way to the lodger through Ivanhoe; the grandmother searches novels for love letters; and the letter scene repeats Rosina’s in The Barber of Seville. Nastenka’s teasing, that he talks as if reading from a book, shows that she can see the difference between literature and life before he can.
themes.development: A society-novel word held back; the catalogue of romantic fantasies; Walter Scott and Pushkin sent downstairs; Ro-si-na hummed over a sealed letter.

themes.name: Anniversaries
themes.summary: Someone looking back on nights possible only when we are young tells this story, and the narrator is already a man who lives in remembrance. He keeps anniversaries of his own sensations, visits places where he was once happy in his own way, and expects to remember these four nights all his life. Nastenka promises the same in her letter. The ending turns memory into a blessing: he will not reproach her, and one moment of happiness is what he keeps.
themes.development: Such a night as is only possible when we are young; the anniversary of that which never existed; where have you buried your best days?; the memory of you in Nastenka’s letter; a whole moment of happiness.

techniques.name: Looking back
techniques.definition: An account given after the event by a narrator who already knows how it ends.
techniques.inThisBook: From the first sentence the nights belong to youth, told by an older man to a dear reader. The Third Night and the Morning slip into the present tense, as if written on the day, so the reader waits for the lodger with the narrator without knowing that he will come.

techniques.name: Address to the reader
techniques.definition: A speaker turning to address the reader, or someone within the story, directly.
techniques.inThisBook: Dear reader on the first page, and then Nastenka, dear Nastenka, over and over: much of the story is spoken to her, and the narrator admits he could never tire of saying her name. The last paragraph speaks to her directly, blessing her on her wedding day.

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.definition: Giving human feelings, speech or action to things.
techniques.inThisBook: Petersburg’s houses greet the narrator, announce their repairs and cry out that they are being painted yellow. Nature in spring is a consumptive girl who is lovely for a moment. A man with no human friends makes friends of buildings, and the joke explains his loneliness.

techniques.name: The dreamer’s monologue
techniques.definition: A long passage built to stand out from the narrative around it.
techniques.inThisBook: Most of the second night is one speech, delivered as though read from a manuscript. It moves from comedy (the snail, the embarrassed visitor, the kitten under a chair) to fantasy and then to real grief about wasted years, and Nastenka’s response, a question about whether he has lived like that all his life, changes the story’s direction.

techniques.name: Third-person self-address
techniques.definition: A speaker referring to himself as he or by a type-name instead of I.
techniques.inThisBook: Asked for his history, the narrator says he is a type and tells his life as our hero, because it is too shaming to say I. The distance lets him be exact about himself, and Nastenka sees through it immediately: this must have happened to you, word for word.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: A reference to another work, person or event that the reader is expected to recognise.
techniques.inThisBook: The dreamer’s fantasies name Hoffmann, Scott’s Diana Vernon, Clara Mowbray, Effie Deans and Minna and Brenda, Meyerbeer’s Robert the Devil, Pushkin’s Egyptian Nights and his little house in Kolomna. Rossini’s Barber of Seville runs through Nastenka’s story, and her ready-written letter is Rosina’s.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Letters written, carried or read within a story.
techniques.inThisBook: A letter is drafted by the narrator, Nastenka hands him one already sealed, he delivers it, and no reply comes. The story ends with her letter to him, which he reads over and over: loving, apologetic and announcing her wedding.

techniques.name: Weather
techniques.definition: Weather used to set a mood or to mark a change in the story.
techniques.inThisBook: Starry, bright nights for the first meetings; a gloomy, rainy day like the old age before me for the third; a lovely blue sky and a passing yellow cloud just before the lodger appears; rain beating on the window on the last morning.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in words whose real meaning is different, or letting events contradict what characters expect.
techniques.inThisBook: Nastenka likes him because he has not fallen in love with her; he argues brilliantly that the lodger must be a man of delicate feeling; he points out a beautiful sky at the moment his happiness ends; Matrona cleans the ceiling for a wedding that is not his.

quotations.text: It was a wonderful night, such a night as is only possible when we are young, dear reader.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the story.
quotations.analysis: The opening words settle two things: the teller is looking back, and he is talking to us. When we are young places the four nights in a lost past, so a reader knows before anything happens that this is a memory, perhaps a happy one and certainly an ended one. The tone is warm, confiding and a little self-mocking, like the rest of the story.

quotations.text: For though I had been living almost eight years in Petersburg I had hardly an acquaintance.
quotations.context: He is explaining why the city’s summer exodus makes him feel deserted.
quotations.analysis: His loneliness is stated as a fact and left there. The next sentence, what did I want with acquaintances?, tries to laugh it off, and then he explains that he knows all Petersburg anyway. The pattern of the whole story is here: a painful truth, a joke to cover it, and a fantasy to replace it.

quotations.text: They, of course, do not know me, but I know them.
quotations.context: The people he sees every day at the same time and place.
quotations.analysis: Eight short words hold the whole asymmetry of his life. He has studied the faces of strangers, is glad when they are gay and downcast when they are under a cloud, and they have no idea he exists. The old man on the Fontanka with the gold-knobbed stick is the nearest thing he has to a friend, and they have never spoken.

quotations.text: when I looked at my friend I heard a plaintive, “They are painting me yellow!”
quotations.context: He describes the houses of Petersburg that seem to greet him in the street.
quotations.analysis: A pretty pink house cries out as it is repainted, and he cannot bear to visit his disfigured friend. The fantasy is funny and tender, and it shows how completely buildings have taken the place of people for him. Yellow, the colour he calls that of the Celestial Empire, returns in Nastenka’s yellow hat and the yellow cloud of the fourth night.

quotations.text: should certainly have pronounced the word “Madam!” if I had not known that that exclamation has been uttered a thousand times in every Russian society novel.
quotations.context: He has found the girl crying at the canal railing and wants to speak to her.
quotations.analysis: Even at the moment of action he thinks in literature, and he is stopped by the fear of a cliché. It is a good joke against himself and against the novels of the day. It also costs him the chance to speak, and only the arrival of a drunken gentleman, a plot device of the same society novels, brings them together.

quotations.text: Why, with no one, with an ideal, with the one I dream of in my sleep. I make up regular romances in my dreams.
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: He has told Nastenka he has often been in love, and she asks with whom.
quotations.analysis: He answers with perfect candour, and the candour is his charm. Nastenka laughs, but kindly, and tells him he is his own enemy. The phrase regular romances is the key to his life: he writes novels in his head in which he is the hero, and has never had to test one against a real woman until tonight.

quotations.text: But you mustn’t fall in love with me, I beg you!
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: She agrees to meet him again the next night, on conditions.
quotations.analysis: Nastenka makes the rule, and the reader knows straight away that it will be broken. She is not being coy: she has her own secret, a man she is waiting for, and she needs a friend who wants nothing from her. The condition gives the story its tension, since every tender moment afterwards has to be passed off as friendship.

quotations.text: I have lived, as they say, keeping myself to myself, that is, utterly alone—alone, entirely alone.
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: Nastenka has asked for his history, and he insists he has none.
quotations.analysis: He repeats the word as if hearing it for the first time. A man who has no history in the ordinary sense, no events and no people, has to explain himself some other way, and this admission leads straight into his great speech about the dreamer. Nastenka’s answer, that she too is shut in with a blind grandmother, begins their likeness.

quotations.text: The dreamer—if you want an exact definition—is not a human being, but a creature of an intermediate sort.
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: He begins his account of the dreamers who live in the strange nooks of Petersburg.
quotations.analysis: Dostoevsky had used almost the same words in a newspaper feuilleton of 1847, the Petersburg Chronicle, where the dreamer becomes a strange creature of the neuter gender. Here the definition is given with mock pedantry by a dreamer about himself. The comparisons that follow, a snail and a tortoise, are comic, and they also show a man who has made himself a shell with no door.

quotations.text: for allow me, Nastenka, to tell my story in the third person, for one feels awfully ashamed to tell it in the first person
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: Halfway through describing the dreamer’s evening walk home.
quotations.analysis: He names the device while using it. Shame makes him call himself our hero, and the move is itself a dreamer’s habit, making a story out of a life. It also lets him be ruthlessly accurate: in the third person he can describe the flushing, the lies to save appearances and the dinner eaten without noticing.

quotations.text: A fresh dream—fresh happiness! A fresh rush of delicate, voluptuous poison!
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: Alone in his room after dinner, the dreamer feels a new fantasy beginning.
quotations.analysis: Happiness and poison sit side by side, and the exclamation marks show a man who cannot give up the drug he is describing. Dostoevsky makes dreaming an addiction: it is sweet, it is solitary, and it leaves the room dark and the soul empty when it fades. The monologue is a confession, and this is its most honest line.

quotations.text: of friendship with Hoffmann, St. Bartholomew’s Night, of Diana Vernon, of playing the hero at the taking of Kazan by Ivan Vassilyevitch, of Clara Mowbray, of Effie Deans
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: Nastenka might ask what the dreamer dreams of; he tells her.
quotations.analysis: Dostoevsky added this list when he revised the story for his collected works of 1860. It is a young man’s reading of the 1830s and 1840s: the German fantasist Hoffmann, three heroines of Walter Scott, a massacre from French history and a Russian victory of 1552. The jumble is the point. Nothing connects these dreams except that he is the hero of every one.

quotations.text: You talk as though you were reading it out of a book.
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: She interrupts his account of the dreamer.
quotations.analysis: Nastenka hits the mark. His eloquence is borrowed, and his life is lived at second hand from books; she hears both. Her plainness is one of the story’s pleasures, and it is why the narrator falls for her: she is the first person who has interrupted his fantasies with the real world, and she does it with affection.

quotations.text: Do you know that I am forced now to celebrate the anniversary of my own sensations, the anniversary of that which was once so sweet, which never existed in reality
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: Near the end of his speech, as comedy gives way to grief.
quotations.analysis: He keeps anniversaries of feelings, and some of them are feelings for things that never happened. It is the saddest idea in the story, and the most exact description of what a life of daydreams leaves behind. The speech has turned from mockery to confession, and Nastenka, who was laughing at the beginning, is now wiping away a tear.

quotations.text: she took a pin and pinned my dress to hers, and said that we should sit like that for the rest of our lives if, of course, I did not become a better girl.
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: After some unnamed mischief at fifteen, her blind grandmother takes precautions.
quotations.analysis: Nothing in the book is funnier or sadder than the pin. A blind woman who cannot watch the girl fastens her to herself, and for two years they sit knitting and reading aloud. Nastenka tells it lightly and scolds the narrator for laughing at her grandmother. The picture of a young life held still explains everything she does next.

quotations.text: But look under the binding; they sometimes stuff it under the bindings, the rascals!
quotations.speaker: The grandmother
quotations.context: The lodger has sent down a parcel of Walter Scott’s novels.
quotations.analysis: She fears the right thing in the wrong place. There is no love letter in the binding; the books themselves are the courtship, and within a month Nastenka is reading Ivanhoe and Pushkin and has stopped dreaming of Chinese princes. The grandmother, who admits to reading such novels all night herself, is one of the story’s best comic turns.

quotations.text: Listen, Nastenka, I can’t do anything; I am a poor man, for I have nothing, not even a decent berth. How could we live, if I were to marry you?
quotations.speaker: The lodger
quotations.context: Nastenka has come to his room with her clothes in a bundle on the night before he leaves.
quotations.analysis: Honest and cautious, the lodger gives money as his reason. He will not take her with him, and he will not bind her with a promise; he says only that he will come back in a year if his position allows. Readers divide over him. His care can look like coldness, and his three days’ silence in Petersburg is never explained.

quotations.text: “R, o—Ro; s, i—si; n, a—na,” I began. “Rosina!” we both hummed together
quotations.context: He has been drafting a letter for her to send, and she hands him one already written and sealed.
quotations.analysis: The joke comes from The Barber of Seville, the opera the lodger took her to: Figaro urges Rosina to write to her lover, and she produces a letter she has already written. Nastenka has been ahead of the narrator all along, and they both know the scene. It is their happiest moment, and it is spent helping her reach another man.

quotations.text: To-day was a gloomy, rainy day without a glimmer of sunlight, like the old age before me.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the Third Night, written the day after.
quotations.analysis: Here the tense changes, and so does the weather. The story is now being written on the day, in the rain, by a man who has begun to guess the truth. At twenty-six he speaks of old age as if it had arrived, and the comparison shows how quickly hope has gone out of him since the evening before.

quotations.text: I like you because you have not fallen in love with me.
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: She is happy, sure that the lodger will answer her letter tonight.
quotations.analysis: She says it to the one man in Petersburg who has fallen in love with her, and he has to hear it. Nastenka is not cruel; she is happy and generous and blind, as he says a moment later. The line is the story’s sharpest piece of dramatic irony, and its cost falls entirely on the listener.

quotations.text: Why isn’t he you? Why isn’t he like you? He is not as good as you, though I love him more than you.
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: The lodger has not come, and she is comparing the two men.
quotations.analysis: Nastenka puts the difference between goodness and love more plainly than any argument could. The narrator is kinder and she knows it; she loves the other man, and she knows that too. The line returns in her final letter, reversed: if only you were he.

quotations.text: Tell me, how is it that we can’t all be like brothers together?
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: She says she is speaking in general now, about everyone.
quotations.analysis: Her simple question gives the story’s idea of love at its widest: people hide what they feel for fear of doing their feelings an injustice, and so everyone seems harsher than he is. Nastenka wants openness, and she is being open with the narrator. The pity is that the brotherhood she offers is exactly what he cannot accept.

quotations.text: It’s impossible, but I love you, Nastenka! There it is! Now everything is told,
quotations.speaker: The dreamer
quotations.context: There is no letter from the lodger, and Nastenka is weeping at the railing.
quotations.analysis: After three nights of eloquence the confession is short and clumsy, accompanied by a wave of the hand. Nastenka’s answer is that she knew long ago. For a few pages the impossible becomes possible: she says she will get over the lodger, and they make plans for the empty room upstairs and another night at the opera.

quotations.text: Oh, my God! If only I could love you both at once! Oh, if only you were he!
quotations.speaker: Nastenka
quotations.context: Her letter, which Matrona brings on the wet morning after.
quotations.analysis: Her letter reverses her question of the third night, why isn’t he you?, and makes it a wish that cannot come true. She is sincere, and she is also asking to be forgiven so that she can be happy with a clear heart. The narrator hears his own words echoed back, and chooses to bless her.

quotations.text: I have taken all the cobwebs off the ceiling; you can have a wedding or give a party.
quotations.speaker: Matrona
quotations.context: He has just read Nastenka’s letter and hidden his face.
quotations.analysis: The servant with no imagination makes the story’s most painful joke without knowing it. The spider’s web he complained about on the first page is gone, and the room is ready for a wedding that belongs to someone else. Suddenly he pictures Matrona grown old, the house opposite peeling, and himself in the same room fifteen years on.

quotations.text: I saw myself just as I was now, fifteen years hence, older, in the same room, just as solitary, with the same Matrona grown no cleverer for those fifteen years.
quotations.context: Rain on the window, and the room suddenly looking old.
quotations.analysis: His future appears as the present repeated. Nothing will change except age, and even the servant will be no cleverer. It is the dreamer’s fear from the second night coming true, and it is also, perhaps, where the teller of the story is writing from: the first sentence said such nights are possible only when we are young.

quotations.text: My God, a whole moment of happiness! Is that too little for the whole of a man’s life?
quotations.context: The last lines of the story, after he has blessed Nastenka.
quotations.analysis: Two answers are possible. It may be gratitude, a moment of real happiness being more than a dreamer ever expected; or it may be despair, since one moment is all he will get. Dostoevsky ends on the question mark and does not choose, and readers have heard the line as consolation and as lament ever since.

timeline.label: Peter the Great founds St Petersburg on the Neva
timeline.detail: The new capital rose on marshland at about sixty degrees north, far enough north for the summer sky to stay light all night for several weeks around midsummer.

timeline.label: Fyodor Dostoevsky is born in Moscow
timeline.detail: The son of a doctor at the Mariinsky Hospital for the poor.

timeline.label: Turgenev’s poem The Flower
timeline.detail: Dostoevsky took the epigraph of White Nights from it, slightly altered and put as a question about staying even a moment near another’s heart.

timeline.label: Poor Folk and The Double
timeline.detail: Dostoevsky’s first two books, one a novel in letters between a poor clerk and a young woman.

timeline.label: The Petersburg Chronicle feuilletons
timeline.detail: Newspaper pieces in which Dostoevsky described the Petersburg dreamer, a strange creature of the neuter gender, in terms the story would repeat.

timeline.label: White Nights appears in Otechestvennye zapiski
timeline.detail: In the December issue, signed F. Dostoevsky and dedicated to the poet Aleksei Pleshcheyev.

timeline.label: Arrest and mock execution
timeline.detail: Dostoevsky and Pleshcheyev were arrested in April with other members of the Petrashevsky circle. In December Dostoevsky was led out to be shot, reprieved at the last moment, and sent to hard labour in Siberia.

timeline.label: Druzhinin reviews the story
timeline.detail: In January’s Sovremennik the critic Aleksandr Druzhinin ranked it above several of Dostoevsky’s earlier stories, while wishing the dreamer had a clearer place, time and occupation.

timeline.label: The revised text
timeline.detail: For his first collected works Dostoevsky revised the style and added the passage listing the dreamer’s romantic fantasies.

timeline.label: Dobrolyubov’s Downtrodden People
timeline.detail: The radical critic saw the dreamer as an early version of the narrator of The Insulted and Injured, and mocked romantic lovers who run errands for their rivals.

timeline.label: Constance Garnett’s translation
timeline.detail: White Nights and Other Stories, the tenth volume of her Novels of Fyodor Dostoevsky, which also contains Notes from Underground.

timeline.label: Visconti’s Le notti bianche
timeline.detail: Marcello Mastroianni and Maria Schell in a modern Italian port town recreated on the sound stages of Cinecittà; the film won the Silver Lion at Venice.

timeline.label: Bresson’s Four Nights of a Dreamer
timeline.detail: Robert Bresson moved the story to contemporary Paris and the embankments of the Seine.

places.name: Catherine Canal (now the Griboyedov Canal), St Petersburg
places.note: Russian commentators take the canal embankment where the narrator finds Nastenka to be this one.

places.name: Fontanka, St Petersburg
places.note: Where he meets the old man with the gold-knobbed stick every day, and where peasants sleep in their barges.

places.name: Nevsky Prospect, St Petersburg
places.note: The main street, one of the walks on which he looks in vain for familiar faces.

places.name: Kamenny Island, St Petersburg
places.note: One of the islands of elegant summer villas to which the city departs, leaving him behind.

places.name: Kolomna, St Petersburg
places.note: The quarter of Pushkin’s The Little House in Kolomna, which appears among the dreamer’s fantasies as a little home of one’s own.

criticalViews.summary: The first reviewers liked it best of Dostoevsky’s early work, and many readers since have loved it as a lyrical story of two young people in a luminous city, with a painful but generous ending. The dreamer’s blessing and the final question are read as the heart of it: a moment of happiness honestly received.
criticalViews.counter: The subtitle calls it sentimental, and the narrator mocks his own feelings as often as he indulges them. Read closely, the story is also a study of a condition Dostoevsky thought damaging, and the warm ending may be the dreamer’s last and best daydream.

criticalViews.summary: On this view the story belongs with the Petersburg Chronicle of 1847 and with Dostoevsky’s later heroes, from the narrator of The Insulted and Injured to the Underground Man, all of them people who live in their heads and cannot join real life. Nastenka matters as the test the dreamer fails, and the ending as a diagnosis.
criticalViews.counter: Treating him as a case loses the comedy and the tenderness, and it undervalues Nastenka, who has her own story and her own choice. The narrator is also self-aware in a way a case study is not: he diagnoses himself on the second night, with more wit than any critic.

criticalViews.summary: Some readers put Nastenka at the centre. She has been shut in for two years, takes the first step with the lodger, writes her letter before being told how, sets the terms with the narrator and decides the ending. Seen this way the dreamer is a charming go-between in a love story that was always hers.
criticalViews.counter: Everything we know of her comes through the narrator’s telling, including her own history, which he reports in her voice. Her letter at the end is sincere, but it also asks him to go on loving her as a brother, which some readers find thoughtless, and Dobrolyubov was scornful of the lover who carries such messages.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dostoevsky present the dreamer, and does the story condemn his way of life?
plan: Begin with the first night: the city emptying, the faces and houses he knows, I know them but they do not know me.
Analyse the second-night monologue: the snail, the embarrassed visitor, the list of fantasies, voluptuous poison.
Show the turn from comedy to grief: the anniversary of sensations and the question where have you buried your best days?
Weigh the real nights against the dreamed ones: what Nastenka gives him and what he loses.
End with the morning: the cleaned ceiling, fifteen years hence, and the double meaning of the last question.

essayQuestions.question: What part does St Petersburg play in White Nights?
plan: The city as the narrator’s only acquaintance: the talking houses and the summer exodus.
The white nights themselves: light, unreality, and meetings that seem to happen outside ordinary time.
Places: the canal railing and the bench, Nastenka’s side street, his green-walled room.
Weather as structure: starlight, rain on the third day, the yellow cloud, the wet morning.
Compare with Gogol’s Petersburg in The Overcoat, or with Dostoevsky’s later Petersburg in Notes from Underground.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Nastenka her own person in the story, and how far is she part of the dreamer’s imagination?
plan: What she does: pinned to her grandmother, the bundle on the lodger’s bed, the letter already written.
How she speaks: teasing, direct, you talk as though you were reading it out of a book.
The limits: everything reaches us through his narration, including her history in her own words.
The fourth night and the morning letter: her choice, and how the narrator responds.
Conclude on whose story this is, and what the title’s white nights suggest about reality and dream.

discussionQuestions: Why does the narrator tell his own history in the third person?
Nastenka makes him promise not to fall in love with her. Was it fair to ask?
Is the lodger a hero, a villain or neither?
Why does the narrator agree to deliver Nastenka’s letter to the man she loves?
Is the last question of the story grateful or despairing?
What would be lost if the story were told by Nastenka?

related.why: Garnett printed them in the same volume: another Petersburg dreamer sixteen years later, grown bitter, telling the story of his own meeting with a young woman.
Gogol’s Petersburg a few years earlier, and another lonely official whose one object of love is something he cannot keep.
The sentimental novel of an earlier generation: a young man who loves a woman promised to another, and lives too much in his own feelings.
Dostoevsky’s last novel, written thirty years and a Siberian prison later, where the questions about love and brotherhood that Nastenka asks come back at full length.
